title: Practice Exam 1
description: A full-length 36-question simulated California Class C knowledge exam. Challenging level.

questions.question: You are on a two-lane highway posted at 55 mph in light rain with moderate traffic. The fastest you may legally drive is:
choices: Whatever speed is safe for the conditions, which may be well below 55 mph
55 mph, because that is the posted maximum
45 mph, the automatic wet-weather limit
No more than 10 mph under the posted limit
questions.explanation: Under the Basic Speed Law you may never drive faster than is safe for current conditions. The posted limit is the maximum for ideal conditions only; there is no fixed 'wet-weather' or 'minus-10' rule.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Basic Speed Law

questions.question: You approach an uncontrolled railroad crossing where buildings block your view of the tracks until you are close. The maximum speed allowed is:
choices: 15 mph
20 mph
25 mph
10 mph
questions.explanation: Within 100 feet of a railroad crossing where you cannot see the tracks for 400 feet in both directions, the limit is 15 mph. The same 15 mph applies at blind intersections and in alleys.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — 15 mph Speed Limits

questions.question: A driver ahead of you brakes hard. To know whether you are following at a safe distance, you should:
choices: Pick a fixed point the car ahead passes and count at least 3 seconds before you reach it
Stay exactly two car lengths back at any speed
Keep a half-second gap so you don't lose your place in traffic
Measure 100 feet of space regardless of speed
questions.explanation: The 3-second rule adjusts automatically for speed, unlike a fixed car-length or distance. Increase it to 4+ seconds in rain, fog, or when followed too closely.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — The 3-Second Rule

questions.question: At night on an open highway you are following another vehicle. You must dim your high beams to low beams when you come within:
choices: 300 feet of the vehicle you are following
500 feet of the vehicle you are following
150 feet of the vehicle you are following
1,000 feet of the vehicle you are following
questions.explanation: Dim your high beams within 300 feet when following another vehicle, and within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle. Mixing these two distances up is a common error.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Using Your Headlights

questions.question: You and an oncoming car reach an intersection at the same time. You are going straight; the oncoming driver is turning left across your path. Who has the right of way?
choices: You do; the left-turning driver must yield to oncoming traffic
The left-turning driver, because they arrived first
Whoever signals first
The oncoming driver, because they are turning
questions.explanation: A driver turning left must yield to vehicles coming straight from the opposite direction (unless they have a green arrow). Going straight, you have the right of way.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Left Turns / Right-of-Way

questions.question: On a city street you must give a continuous turn signal for the last 100 feet before turning. On the freeway, you should signal for at least:
choices: 5 seconds before changing lanes
100 feet before changing lanes
2 seconds before changing lanes
10 seconds before changing lanes
questions.explanation: Freeway lane changes call for a 5-second signal (time-based) because of higher speeds, while turns on surface streets use the 100-foot (distance-based) rule.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Signaling

questions.question: Before you move from your lane to the left, the LAST thing you should do just before steering over is:
choices: Glance over your left shoulder to check the blind spot
Check your rear-view mirror
Check your left side mirror
Turn on your signal
questions.explanation: Signal, then mirrors, and finally a head-check of the blind spot immediately before moving—mirrors alone don't show the blind spot. The shoulder glance is the final step.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Changing Lanes

questions.question: Total stopping distance is longest because it is made up of:
choices: Perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance combined
Only the distance your car travels once the brakes grab
Only the distance you travel during your reaction time
The length of the car plus one car length of space
questions.explanation: You travel during the time it takes to see a hazard (perception), to move your foot to the brake (reaction), AND while the brakes slow the car. All three grow rapidly with speed.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Stopping Distances

questions.question: A 22-year-old driver has a BAC of 0.06%. Regarding driving, this driver:
choices: Can still be arrested for DUI if impaired, even though under 0.08%
Is completely safe and legal because it is under 0.08%
Is only breaking the law if under 21
Cannot be charged unless a crash occurs
questions.explanation: 0.08% is the level at which you are presumed too impaired to drive, but you can be convicted of DUI at any BAC if your driving is impaired. Alcohol affects you well before 0.08%.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Alcohol and Driving

questions.question: By driving in California you have given 'implied consent.' This means that if you are lawfully arrested for DUI and refuse a chemical test:
choices: Your license will be suspended automatically, separate from the DUI case
Nothing happens unless you are later convicted
You simply pay a small fee to reinstate it
The arrest is dismissed because testing is voluntary
questions.explanation: Under the implied consent law, refusing a breath or blood test after a lawful DUI arrest triggers an automatic license suspension and added penalties, independent of the DUI charge itself.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Implied Consent Law

questions.question: A school bus on the OTHER side of an undivided two-lane road stops and flashes red lights. You must:
choices: Stop and stay stopped until the red lights stop flashing
Slow to 25 mph and pass with caution
Continue, because the bus is in the opposite lane
Stop only if you see children in the road
questions.explanation: On an undivided road, both directions must stop for a bus flashing red lights. You may proceed without stopping only when a raised median or barrier divides the roadway.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — School Buses

questions.question: You are driving 25 mph past a school at recess. A ball bounces into the street ahead. The best response is to:
choices: Cover the brake and slow further, expecting a child to run out after it
Maintain 25 mph since it is the legal limit
Swerve into the oncoming lane to go around it
Sound your horn and keep your speed
questions.explanation: A ball in the road is a classic warning that a child may follow without looking. Anticipate the hazard and be ready to stop—obeying the speed limit alone is not enough.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Watching for Children

questions.question: An ambulance with siren and lights approaches while you are stopped in the left lane at a red light, with cars on your right. You should:
choices: Stay put if you cannot safely move right; do not enter the intersection
Drive into the intersection to clear a path
Make a U-turn to get out of the way
Run the red light and pull over past the intersection
questions.explanation: Pull to the right and stop when you safely can, but never enter or block an intersection or run a red light to do so. If you're boxed in, remain stopped and let the emergency vehicle route around you.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Emergency Vehicles

questions.question: Approaching a tow truck stopped on the freeway shoulder with amber lights flashing, the 'Move Over, Slow Down' law requires you to:
choices: Move over a lane if safe; if you can't, slow to a safe and reasonable speed
Maintain your speed since it is only a tow truck
Stop completely until the tow truck leaves
Move over only if a police officer is also present
questions.explanation: The law covers tow trucks and Caltrans vehicles with flashing amber lights, not just police and ambulances. Change lanes away from them when possible; otherwise slow down.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Move Over, Slow Down Law

questions.question: At an intersection with no marked crosswalk, a pedestrian steps off the curb to cross. You:
choices: Must yield; a legal crosswalk exists at intersections even without paint
Have the right of way because the crosswalk is not painted
Must yield only if the pedestrian is in a marked crosswalk
May proceed if you honk first
questions.explanation: An unmarked crosswalk legally exists across each intersection. You must yield to pedestrians crossing there, just as you would at a painted crosswalk.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Pedestrians / Crosswalks

questions.question: You want to pass a bicyclist but the lane is too narrow to leave 3 feet of space. You should:
choices: Slow down and wait until you can pass with at least 3 feet of clearance
Pass anyway as long as you don't touch the cyclist
Honk and squeeze by closely
Pass with 1 foot of space if you are going slowly
questions.explanation: The Three Feet for Safety Act requires at least 3 feet when passing a cyclist. If you can't, you must slow down and wait for a safe gap before passing.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Sharing the Road with Bicyclists

questions.question: You park facing uphill on a street with a curb. To keep the car from rolling into traffic if the brakes fail, turn the front wheels:
choices: Away from the curb, and let the car roll back slightly onto the curb
Toward the curb so the front tire blocks it
Straight, and rely on the parking brake alone
Away from the curb and leave it in neutral
questions.explanation: Uphill WITH a curb: wheels point away from the curb so a backward roll catches the tire against the curb. (Downhill, or uphill with no curb, you point them toward the edge.) Always set the parking brake.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Parking on Hills

questions.question: Which of these is a legal place to park?
choices: 16 feet from a fire hydrant on an unmarked street
Within 10 feet of a fire hydrant
In a crosswalk while you wait for a passenger
On the sidewalk with two wheels off the road
questions.explanation: You may not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, in a crosswalk, or on a sidewalk. 16 feet from a hydrant clears the 15-foot rule.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Where You May Not Park

questions.question: You are entering a freeway from a short on-ramp and traffic is moving fast. The safest action is to:
choices: Accelerate on the ramp to match traffic speed and merge into a gap
Stop at the end of the ramp until a large gap appears
Enter slowly and let freeway traffic adjust to you
Merge at whatever speed you are going and brake if needed
questions.explanation: Use the ramp to reach traffic speed, then merge smoothly into a gap. Stopping or entering too slowly forces fast traffic to brake suddenly and causes crashes.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Entering Freeways

questions.question: You are in a carpool (HOV) lane bordered by a single set of double solid lines and your exit is approaching. You may:
choices: Exit the HOV lane only where the lines become broken (dashed)
Cross the double solid lines wherever your exit is closest
Cross the double lines as long as you signal
Stay in the HOV lane and exit across all lanes at once
questions.explanation: Double solid lines mark the HOV-lane boundary; crossing them is illegal. Enter and exit only where the lines are broken, then change lanes one at a time toward your exit.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Carpool / HOV Lanes

questions.question: Which statement about cell phones while driving in California is correct?
choices: An adult may use a phone only hands-free; a driver under 18 may not use one at all
Anyone may text while stopped at a red light
Adults may hold the phone if the call is under one minute
Hands-free use is illegal for everyone
questions.explanation: Adults must use voice-operated, hands-free mode; drivers under 18 may not use any wireless device, even hands-free. Texting is banned for all drivers, including while stopped at a light.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Cell Phone Laws

questions.question: Glancing down to read a text for about 5 seconds at 55 mph means you travel roughly the length of a football field essentially blind. This illustrates that:
choices: Even a brief glance away covers a long distance at speed
Texting is safe if you only look for a few seconds
Reading is fine as long as you don't type
Speed has little effect on how far you travel while distracted
questions.explanation: At 55 mph you cover about 100 yards in 5 seconds. Any glance away from the road, even a quick one, leaves you driving blind for a surprising distance.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Distracted Driving

questions.question: A traffic light turns yellow as you approach. You are close enough that stopping would require slamming the brakes. You should:
choices: Proceed through the intersection with caution
Brake hard to stop before the line no matter what
Speed up well above the limit to clear it
Stop in the middle of the crosswalk
questions.explanation: Yellow means stop if you can do so safely. If you are too close to stop without risking a rear-end collision, continue through carefully—but never accelerate to 'beat' the light.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Traffic Signal Lights

questions.question: You reach an intersection where the signal is dark due to a power outage. You should treat it as:
choices: A four-way stop—stop, then proceed in turn
A green light, since no red is showing
A yield—slow down but don't stop
Controlled by whoever is biggest or fastest
questions.explanation: When signals are completely dark, the law requires you to treat the intersection as an all-way stop. A flashing red also means stop; a flashing yellow means slow and proceed with caution.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Inoperative / Flashing Signals

questions.question: There is a broken yellow line on your side of the centerline and a solid yellow line on the other side. This means:
choices: You may pass when safe; oncoming traffic may not
Neither direction may pass
Both directions may pass freely
Only oncoming traffic may pass
questions.explanation: A broken yellow line on your side means passing is allowed when safe; the solid line on the other side means that direction may not pass. The line nearest you governs you.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Pavement Markings

questions.question: Approaching a roundabout already occupied by circulating vehicles, you should:
choices: Yield to traffic in the circle, then enter a gap and drive counterclockwise
Come to a full stop and wait for the roundabout to empty
Enter quickly to claim your place before checking
Drive clockwise to reach the nearest exit
questions.explanation: Traffic already in the roundabout has the right of way. Slow, yield, enter when there's a safe gap, keep to the right of the central island (counterclockwise), and signal before exiting.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Roundabouts

questions.question: At a four-way stop, you stop first. The driver to your right stops just after you. You both intend to go straight. Who goes first?
choices: You do, because you stopped first
The driver on the right, always
Both proceed together since you're not crossing paths
The driver who accelerates first
questions.explanation: First to stop, first to go. The 'yield to the right' rule only breaks a tie when two drivers stop at the same time. Here you arrived first, so you proceed first.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Four-Way Stops

questions.question: In dense fog, the best way to improve how well you can see and be seen is to:
choices: Slow down and use low-beam headlights
Turn on your high beams for more light
Use only your parking lights
Turn on your hazard lights while continuing at normal speed
questions.explanation: High beams reflect off fog and worsen glare. Use low beams (or fog lights) and reduce speed. Hazard lights are for a stopped/disabled vehicle, not normal driving.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Driving in Fog

questions.question: You may legally drive in a bike lane:
choices: When making a right turn, within 200 feet of the corner, after yielding to cyclists
Any time, as long as no cyclist is currently in it
Never, under any circumstances
To pass slow traffic during rush hour
questions.explanation: You may merge into a bike lane only to prepare for a right turn, within 200 feet of the corner, and only after checking for and yielding to bicyclists. Otherwise the bike lane is off-limits to cars.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Bicycle Lanes

questions.question: You park facing downhill on a street that has NO curb. You should turn your front wheels:
choices: Toward the edge of the road, so a rolling car leaves the roadway
Toward the center of the road
Away from the edge of the road
Straight, since there is no curb to use
questions.explanation: With no curb (uphill or downhill), aim the wheels toward the edge so a runaway car rolls off the road, not into traffic. A curb changes only the uphill case.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Parking on Hills

questions.question: A five-sided (pentagon) sign with a point on top means:
choices: School zone or school crossing ahead
No passing zone ahead
Hospital ahead
A T-intersection ahead
questions.explanation: The pentagon shape is reserved for school zone / school crossing warnings. A pennant (horizontal triangle) marks no-passing zones; other shapes carry other meanings.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Sign Shapes

questions.question: On a dry day you keep a 3-second following gap. Conditions that should make you increase it to 4 or more seconds include:
choices: Wet roads, being tailgated, or following a motorcycle
Driving on a wide, empty road
Light traffic in good weather
Traveling below the speed limit
questions.explanation: Add following distance when traction or visibility drops, when a tailgater is behind you (so you can brake gently), or when following a motorcycle, which can stop quickly.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Following Distance

questions.question: You feel fine after two beers an hour ago. The only thing that actually lowers your blood alcohol level is:
choices: Time, while your body breaks the alcohol down
Drinking coffee to wake up
Eating a large meal
A cold shower and fresh air
questions.explanation: Only time reduces BAC. Coffee, food, and showers may make you feel more alert but do not make you sober or safe to drive—'feeling fine' is itself an effect of impairment.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Alcohol and the Body

questions.question: A pedestrian using a white cane steps into the roadway at a corner. You must:
choices: Stop and yield completely; they have the right of way at all times
Edge forward so they know you are there
Honk to alert them and proceed
Continue, since you reached the corner first
questions.explanation: A pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog always has the right of way. Stop well back and stay quiet—honking or creeping forward can disorient them.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Pedestrians with Disabilities

questions.question: You are about to change lanes when you notice a car you can no longer see in your mirrors. You should:
choices: Wait—it is likely in your blind spot; do not change lanes
Change lanes; if it were close you would see it in the mirror
Speed up and move over before it reappears
Change lanes slowly so it has time to brake
questions.explanation: A vehicle that vanishes from your mirrors is usually in your blind spot. Hold your lane and do a shoulder check; never move over based on mirrors alone.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Blind Spots

questions.question: Your light turns green, but a car that ran the late yellow is still crossing the intersection. You should:
choices: Yield and wait until the intersection is clear before proceeding
Proceed immediately because you now have the green
Accelerate to assert your right of way
Honk and edge into the intersection
questions.explanation: A green light means go only when the intersection is clear. You must still yield to vehicles and pedestrians already in it, even when you have the right of way.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Traffic Signal Lights
